title: Self-Concept and Self-Esteem
summary: What self-concept and self-esteem are, factors that influence them, signs of high and low self-esteem, and practical ways to build a positive self-image.

notes.text: The picture you have of yourself: your beliefs about your abilities, appearance, personality, values and roles.
How much you value, respect and like yourself; how you feel about your self-concept.
How you see yourself, especially your appearance. It may be different from how others see you.

rows: Family
Parents who praise effort and listen help children feel valued; constant criticism can damage self-esteem
Friends and peers
Acceptance by friends builds confidence; being excluded or bullied hurts
School and teachers
Achievements, encouragement and fair treatment
Media and social media
Edited photos and influencers can create unrealistic ideas of beauty and success
Culture and religion
Values and expectations about who you should be
Your own thoughts
Negative self-talk ('I'm useless') versus positive self-talk ('I can learn this')

notes.title: Finding the influence
notes.problem: Naledi's coach praises her effort, but classmates mock her accent. How could each affect her self-concept?
steps: Teasing can make her doubt herself.
She can choose whose opinions to value.
notes.answer: Both shape how she sees herself, and she can choose what to believe.

rows: Accept themselves, including their weaknesses
Feel worthless or not good enough
Try new things and are not afraid of mistakes
Avoid challenges because they fear failure
Can say no to peer pressure
Give in to pressure to be accepted
Accept compliments and criticism calmly
Brush off compliments and are hurt by criticism
Respect other people
May bully others or allow others to bully them

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Healthy self-esteem is not arrogance. Arrogant people think they are better than others; people with healthy self-esteem value themselves **and** others.

items: **Know your strengths**: make a list of your talents, skills and good qualities.
**Set realistic goals** and celebrate small achievements.
**Use positive self-talk**: replace 'I always fail' with 'I'll try a different way next time'.
**Look after your body**: exercise, sleep and healthy food improve mood.
**Limit comparison** on social media; remember that images are often edited.
**Help others**: volunteering builds a sense of purpose.

notes.text: A **SMART** goal is **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**ealistic and **T**ime-bound. Example: 'I will improve my Maths mark from 55% to 65% by the end of Term 2 by doing 30 minutes of practice exercises four times a week.'

notes.title: A SMART goal
notes.problem: Turn 'I want to read more' into a SMART goal.
steps: Achievable and relevant: suits your time and aim.
notes.answer: 'I will read one book a month from now until December.'

questions.prompt: What is the difference between self-concept and self-esteem?
questions.memo:
✓ Self-concept is the picture/beliefs you have about yourself (1)
✓ Self-esteem is how much you value and like yourself (1)

questions.prompt: Which is most likely to LOWER a teenager's self-esteem?
options: Comparing themselves with edited social media photos

questions.prompt: Having healthy self-esteem means thinking you are better than everyone else.
In a SMART goal, what does the T stand for?

pairs.left: Tries new things without fear of mistakes
Gives in to pressure to be accepted

questions.prompt: Rewrite this negative self-talk as positive self-talk: 'I'm terrible at sport, so there's no point trying.'
questions.memo: ✓✓ Any positive, realistic rewrite, e.g. 'I'm still learning; if I practise, I will improve and enjoy it more.' (2)

questions.prompt: Suggest THREE ways a learner can build healthy self-esteem.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): know your strengths; set realistic goals; positive self-talk; accept mistakes; supportive friends; exercise and sleep; limit comparison; help others

questions.prompt: Write a SMART goal for improving your reading.
questions.memo:
✓ Specific and measurable (e.g. read one novel / 20 pages a day) (1)
✓ Achievable and realistic (1)
✓ Time-bound (e.g. by the end of the term) (1)

questions.prompt: Explain how social media can affect a teenager's self-image.
questions.memo:
✓ Edited photos and influencers show unrealistic standards of beauty or success (1)
✓ Comparing yourself to them can make you feel inadequate / lower self-esteem (1)

questions.prompt: Give TWO ways in which a family can help a teenager develop a positive self-concept.
questions.memo: Any two (1 each): praise effort; listen; show love and support; set fair rules; encourage independence; avoid harsh criticism
